items.prose: A seed firm tests whether a new fertiliser raises wheat yield. A plot's yield has a known sd of 1.2 tonnes a hectare. A trial of 36 plots runs a one-sided $z$ test at 5%, rejecting when $z > 1.645$. If the fertiliser works, it adds 0.45 tonnes a hectare.

parts.question: If the fertiliser works, where is $z$ centred for a trial of 36 plots? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The standard error is $\tfrac{1.2}{\sqrt{36}} = 0.2$, so the centre is $\tfrac{0.45}{0.2} = 2.25$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Under $H_1$, $z$ is centred at the effect over the standard error, $\tfrac{\delta\sqrt n}{\sigma}$.

byKey.over-sd: You divided by the sd of one plot. The mean of 36 plots has standard error $\tfrac{1.2}{6} = 0.2$.
byKey.over-n: You divided the sd by 36. The standard error divides by $\sqrt{36} = 6$.

explain.text: A true gain of 0.45 is $\tfrac{0.45}{0.2} = 2.25$ standard errors. So under $H_1$, $z$ is normal with mean 2.25 and sd 1.

parts.question: Using the centre 2.25 from part 1, what is the power of one 36-plot trial? You are told $\Phi(0.605) = 0.7274$ and $\Phi(2.25) = 0.9878$. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Power is the area of the $H_1$ curve past the cut-off.

byKey.beta: That is $\beta$, the chance of missing a working fertiliser. Power is $1 - \beta$.
byKey.alpha: That is $\alpha$, the chance of rejecting when the fertiliser does nothing. Power is the chance of rejecting when it works.
byKey.centre-only: That is $\Phi$ at the centre itself. Power is the area past the cut-off, so subtract 1.645 first: $\Phi(2.25 - 1.645)$.

explain.text: Under $H_1$ the cut-off sits $2.25 - 1.645 = 0.605$ below the centre. So the trial rejects with chance $\Phi(0.605) = 0.7274$.

parts.question: The firm could run two independent 36-plot trials, launching if either rejects. Suppose the fertiliser works. Using the power 0.7274 from part 2, what is the chance that at least one rejects? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Both miss with chance $(1 - 0.7274)^2 = 0.2726^2 = 0.0743$, so at least one rejects with chance $1 - 0.0743 = 0.9257$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the chance that both trials miss, then take its complement.

byKey.both: That is the chance both reject, $0.7274^2$. Either one is enough, so take 1 minus the chance both miss.
byKey.added: You added the two powers. Chances of events that can both happen do not add; use 1 minus the chance both miss.
byKey.carried: You used 0.2726 as the power, which is $\beta$. With power 0.7274 both miss with chance $0.2726^2$, so the answer is 0.9257.

explain.text: The trials are independent, so both miss with chance $0.2726^2 = 0.0743$. The either rule finds a working fertiliser with chance 0.9257.

parts.question: Instead, the firm could run one trial of 72 plots at the same 5% level. Using the centre 2.25 for 36 plots from part 1, its centre is $2.25\sqrt 2$. You are told $\Phi(1.537) = 0.9379$ and $\Phi(3.182) = 0.9993$. What is its power? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The centre is $2.25\sqrt 2 \approx 3.182$, which is $1.537$ past 1.645, so the power is $\Phi(1.537) = 0.9379$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the cut-off from the new centre and read $\Phi$ there.

byKey.beta: That is the chance the 72-plot trial misses. Power is $\Phi(1.537) = 0.9379$ itself.
byKey.unchanged: That is the power of 36 plots. Doubling the plots moves the centre to $2.25\sqrt 2 = 3.182$.
byKey.centre-only: That is $\Phi$ at the centre, 3.182. Subtract the cut-off first: $\Phi(3.182 - 1.645) = \Phi(1.537)$.

explain.text: Doubling $n$ multiplies the centre by $\sqrt 2$, to 3.182. The cut-off is 1.537 below it, so one 72-plot trial rejects with chance 0.9379.

parts.question: Using parts 3 and 4, which plan should the firm choose? A fertiliser that does nothing passes the either rule with chance $1 - 0.95^2 = 0.0975$.

options.text: One 72-plot trial: more power, 0.9379 against 0.9257, and $\alpha = 0.05$ against 0.0975
Two trials with the either rule, since it gives two chances to find the gain
options.why: Two chances also nearly double the risk of launching a useless fertiliser, to 0.0975. And its power, 0.9257, is below the single trial's 0.9379.

options.text: Two trials, launching only if both reject, as that rules out luck
options.why: Requiring both cuts the power to $0.7274^2 = 0.5291$, far below one trial of 72 plots.

options.text: Either plan, since both use 72 plots in all
options.why: The plots are the same but the rules differ. One test on 72 plots has the higher power and the lower $\alpha$.

feedback.correct: The single trial has power 0.9379 and $\alpha = 0.05$; the either rule has power 0.9257 and $\alpha = 0.0975$. One large trial wins on both errors.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare both errors for each plan: the power, and the chance of passing a useless fertiliser.

byKey.either: Two chances also nearly double the risk of launching a useless fertiliser, to 0.0975. And its power, 0.9257, is below the single trial's 0.9379.
byKey.both: Requiring both cuts the power to $0.7274^2 = 0.5291$, far below one trial of 72 plots.
byKey.same: The plots are the same but the rules differ. One test on 72 plots has the higher power and the lower $\alpha$.

explain.text: Pooling the plots moves the centre out by $\sqrt 2$ in a single test, with one chance of a false pass. The either rule gains less power and pays for it with a nearly doubled $\alpha$.

items.prose: A fleet manager compares the tread wear of two tyre brands, in mm per 10,000 miles. Brand A on 50 cars wears 3.2 on average, with sd 0.9. Brand B on 40 other cars wears 2.8, with sd 0.6. She tests whether the two mean wears differ, two-sided.

parts.question: What is the standard error of $\bar x_A - \bar x_B$, keeping each brand's own variance? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add $\tfrac{s_A^2}{n_A}$ and $\tfrac{s_B^2}{n_B}$, then take the square root.

byKey.sum-se: You added the two standard errors, 0.1273 and 0.0949. Independent variances add, so add $\tfrac{s^2}{n}$ and then take the root.
byKey.variance: That is the variance of the gap. The standard error is its square root.
byKey.same-n: You divided both variances by 50. Brand B ran on 40 cars, so its variance of the mean is $\tfrac{0.36}{40}$.

explain.text: The two samples are independent, so their variances of the mean add: $0.0162 + 0.009 = 0.0252$. Its root, 0.1587 mm, is Welch's standard error.

parts.question: Using the standard error 0.1587 from part 1, what is Welch's $t$ for A minus B? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the gap in means by its standard error.

byKey.carried: You used 0.2221, the sum of the two standard errors. With 0.1587, $t = 2.520$.
byKey.over-variance: You divided by 0.0252, the variance. Divide the gap by its standard error, 0.1587.

explain.text: The gap is 0.4 mm, which is $\tfrac{0.4}{0.1587} \approx 2.520$ standard errors.

parts.question: With 90 cars, treat $t$ as standard normal. Using $t = 2.520$ from part 2 and $\Phi(2.52) = 0.9941$, what is the two-sided p-value? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Double the tail beyond $|t|$.

byKey.one-sided: That is one tail. The question is whether the wears differ in either direction, so both tails count.
byKey.inside: That is the area between $-2.52$ and 2.52. The p-value is the area outside them.

explain.text: Each tail beyond 2.52 holds $1 - 0.9941 = 0.0059$, and a two-sided test counts both: $p = 0.0118$.

parts.question: Using $p = 0.0118$ from part 3, which statement is right?

options.text: With equal mean wear, a gap at least this large would arise in about 1.2% of trials
There is a 1.2% chance that the two brands wear alike
options.why: A p-value assumes the brands wear alike. It is not the chance that they do.

options.text: Brand A wears far faster, because p is so small
options.why: A small p says the gap is hard to put down to luck. Its size is the 0.4 mm itself, which p does not measure.

options.text: A repeat of the trial would be significant 98.8% of the time
options.why: That would be the power of a repeat trial, which depends on the true gap. $1 - p$ is not the power.

feedback.correct: $p$ is $P(\text{a gap at least this extreme} \mid H_0)$: with equal mean wear, about 1.2% of such trials show a gap this large.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what a p-value assumes before it is computed.

byKey.chance-null: A p-value assumes the brands wear alike. It is not the chance that they do.
byKey.size: A small p says the gap is hard to put down to luck. Its size is the 0.4 mm itself, which p does not measure.
byKey.repeat: That would be the power of a repeat trial, which depends on the true gap. $1 - p$ is not the power.

explain.text: Every p-value is computed in a world where $H_0$ holds. It measures how surprising the data are there, not how likely $H_0$ is or how large the gap is.

items.prose: A shoe maker tests whether its new racing shoe makes runners faster. Nine runners each run the same 5 km course twice on one morning, once in their old shoes and once in the new ones. New time minus old time, in seconds: $-7, -3, -9, -1, -4, -5, 1, -3, -5$. Treat the nine differences as independent draws from a normal distribution.

parts.question: What is the mean difference $\bar d$, in seconds?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the nine differences and divide by 9.

byKey.n-minus-one: You divided the total, $-36$, by 8. The mean divides by the number of runners, 9.
byKey.sign: The differences are new minus old, and most are negative. Their mean is $-4$, not 4.

explain.text: The nine differences sum to $-36$, so $\bar d = -4$: the new shoe is 4 seconds faster on average.

parts.question: Using $\bar d = -4$ from part 1, what is the sd $s_d$ of the differences, dividing by $n - 1$?

feedback.correct: The deviations from $-4$ are $-3, 1, -5, 3, 0, -1, 5, 1, -1$. Their squares sum to 72, so $s_d^2 = \tfrac{72}{8} = 9$ and $s_d = 3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each deviation from $-4$, add, divide by 8, then take the square root.

byKey.divide-by-n: You divided 72 by 9. With $\bar d$ estimated from the same data, divide by $n - 1 = 8$.
byKey.variance: That is $s_d^2$. The sd is its square root.
byKey.carried: You measured the deviations from $-4.5$. From $\bar d = -4$ the squares sum to 72, so $s_d = 3$.

explain.text: Dividing by 8 allows for $\bar d$ being fitted to the same nine numbers. So $s_d = \sqrt{\tfrac{72}{8}} = 3$ seconds.

parts.question: Using $\bar d = -4$ and $s_d = 3$, what is the paired $t$ statistic? Give a decimal.

byKey.over-sd: You divided by $s_d$ itself. The mean of 9 differences has standard error $\tfrac{3}{\sqrt 9} = 1$.
byKey.root-eight: You divided $s_d$ by $\sqrt 8$. The curve has 8 degrees of freedom, but the standard error uses $\sqrt 9$.
byKey.carried: You used $s_d = 2.828$, from dividing by 9. With $s_d = 3$ the statistic is $-4$.
byKey.sign: The mean difference is $-4$, so the statistic is negative: the new times are lower.

explain.text: The standard error of $\bar d$ is $\tfrac{3}{\sqrt 9} = 1$ second, so $t = -4$. It follows $t_8$, as nine differences give 8 degrees of freedom.

parts.question: Using $t = -4$ from part 3, which analysis and conclusion are right at 5%? The one-sided 5% cut-off of $t_8$ is 1.860.

options.text: Paired: each runner ran both shoes, and $t = -4$ is below $-1.860$, so reject $H_0$
Welch's test on the old times against the new, as two groups of 9
options.why: The groups are not independent: each new time has a partner run by the same runner. Pairing cancels the spread between runners.

options.text: A $z$ test with cut-off 1.645, as the gain of 4 seconds is known
options.why: The sd of the differences was estimated from 9 runners, so $t$ follows $t_8$ and the cut-off is 1.860.

options.text: Paired, but fail to reject, because nine runners are too few
options.why: Nine runners can be enough when the differences are steady. $t = -4$ is well past $-1.860$.

feedback.correct: Each runner is their own control, so the test is paired. $t = -4$ is far below $-1.860$, so the new shoe is faster at 5%.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask whether each new time has a natural partner, then compare $t$ with the cut-off.

byKey.welch: The groups are not independent: each new time has a partner run by the same runner. Pairing cancels the spread between runners.
byKey.normal: The sd of the differences was estimated from 9 runners, so $t$ follows $t_8$ and the cut-off is 1.860.
byKey.too-few: Nine runners can be enough when the differences are steady. $t = -4$ is well past $-1.860$.

explain.text: Runners differ from each other by far more than 4 seconds. Pairing takes those differences out, leaving the steady gain, which $t_8$ judges as clear.

parts.question: A larger trial should have 80% power to detect a gain of 1.5 seconds, one-sided at 5%. Using $s_d = 3$ from part 2 as the sd of a difference and $n = 6.18\,(\sigma/\delta)^2$, how many runners does it need? Round up to a whole runner.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out $\tfrac{\sigma}{\delta}$, square it, multiply by 6.18, then round up.

byKey.not-rounded: That is $n$ before rounding. A trial needs whole runners, and 24 fall short, so round up to 25.
byKey.rounded-down: 24 runners give a little under 80% power. Round up, to 25.
byKey.no-square: You left $\tfrac{\sigma}{\delta} = 2$ unsquared. The sample size grows with its square: $6.18 \times 4$.
byKey.carried: You used $s_d = 2.828$, from dividing by 9. With $s_d = 3$, $n = 6.18 \times 4 = 24.72$, so 25 runners.

explain.text: The paired design uses the sd of a difference, 3 seconds, not the far larger spread between runners. So the normal formula asks for only 25 runners. A $t$ test, with the sd estimated, needs a couple more.

items.prose: A clinic screens patients with a blood marker. In healthy patients the marker is normal with mean 50 and sd 10. With the disease it is normal with mean 72 and sd 10. The clinic flags a patient when the marker is above 68, so $H_0$ is that the patient is healthy. 2% of the patients screened have the disease.

parts.question: What is $\alpha$, the chance that a healthy patient is flagged? You are told $\Phi(1.8) = 0.9641$. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $68$ is $\tfrac{68 - 50}{10} = 1.8$ sds above the healthy mean, so $\alpha = 1 - 0.9641 = 0.0359$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Standardise 68 on the healthy curve and take the area above it.

byKey.lower: That is the chance a healthy patient is not flagged. $\alpha$ is the area above 68.
byKey.two-tail: You counted both tails. A flag needs a high marker only, so take the upper tail.
byKey.disease-curve: That is the chance a patient with the disease is flagged, the power. $\alpha$ uses the healthy curve, mean 50.

explain.text: A type I error flags a healthy patient. On the healthy curve 68 is 1.8 sds up, and the tail beyond it holds 0.0359.

parts.question: Using the same cut-off of 68, what is $\beta$, the chance that a patient with the disease is not flagged? You are told $\Phi(0.4) = 0.6554$. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $68$ is $\tfrac{68 - 72}{10} = -0.4$ sds from the disease mean, so $\beta = \Phi(-0.4) = 1 - 0.6554 = 0.3446$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Standardise 68 on the disease curve and take the area below it.

byKey.power: That is the chance the patient is flagged, the power. $\beta$ is the area below 68 on the disease curve.
byKey.healthy-curve: You used the healthy curve. $\beta$ is about patients with the disease, whose markers centre on 72.

explain.text: A type II error misses a patient with the disease. On that curve 68 sits 0.4 sds below the mean, so $\beta = 0.3446$.

parts.question: Using $\alpha = 0.0359$ from part 1 and $\beta = 0.3446$ from part 2, how many of 10,000 screened patients are flagged on average? Give the nearest whole number.

feedback.correct: $9{,}800 \times 0.0359 = 351.8$ healthy and $200 \times 0.6554 = 131.1$ with the disease: about 483 flags.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the flags in each group: the healthy at rate $\alpha$, the others at rate $1 - \beta$.

byKey.true-only: That counts only the 131 flagged patients with the disease. Add the $9{,}800 \times 0.0359 \approx 352$ healthy patients flagged.
byKey.false-only: That counts only the healthy patients flagged. Add the $200 \times 0.6554 \approx 131$ with the disease who are flagged.
byKey.beta-not-power: You multiplied the 200 by $\beta$. Patients with the disease are flagged with chance $1 - \beta = 0.6554$.

explain.text: Of 10,000 patients, 200 have the disease and 9,800 do not. Flags come from both groups: $351.8 + 131.1 \approx 483$.

parts.question: Part 3 gave about 483 flags, of which 131.1 are patients with the disease. What share of flagged patients have the disease? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the flags with the disease by all the flags.

byKey.flipped: That is the share of flags that are healthy. The question asks for those with the disease, $\tfrac{131.1}{483}$.
byKey.power: That is the power, the chance a patient with the disease is flagged. Here the flag is given and the disease is asked.
byKey.carried: You used 421 flags, from multiplying by $\beta$. With 483 flags and 131.1 true ones the share is 0.27.

explain.text: Healthy patients far outnumber the others, so even a 3.59% rate gives 352 false flags against 131 true ones. Only about 27% of flags have the disease.

parts.question: A patient is flagged. Using the share 0.27 from part 4, which statement is right?

options.text: About 27 in 100 flagged patients have the disease, so a flag calls for a second test
The patient has the disease with chance 0.9641, since healthy markers pass 68 only 3.59% of the time
options.why: 0.0359 is the chance of a flag given health, not of health given a flag. With 2% prevalence, most flags come from healthy patients.

options.text: The patient has the disease with chance 0.6554, the test's power
options.why: Power is the chance of a flag given the disease. The flag is what is known here, so the base rate matters.

options.text: Raising the cut-off would catch more patients with the disease
options.why: A higher cut-off flags fewer patients, so $\beta$ grows and more cases are missed.

feedback.correct: Of 483 flags, 131 have the disease: about 27%. A flag raises the chance from 2% to 27%, so it calls for a follow-up, not a diagnosis.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the share of flags that have the disease, which depends on how rare the disease is.

byKey.one-minus-alpha: 0.0359 is the chance of a flag given health, not of health given a flag. With 2% prevalence, most flags come from healthy patients.
byKey.power: Power is the chance of a flag given the disease. The flag is what is known here, so the base rate matters.
byKey.raise: A higher cut-off flags fewer patients, so $\beta$ grows and more cases are missed.

explain.text: $P(\text{disease} \mid \text{flag})$ turns the test's error rates round with the 2% base rate. It is neither $1 - \alpha$ nor the power.
